utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. This is case number IT-03-67-PT, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Seselj, can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then may I have the -- we are here for a Status Conference. My screen is not ... Yes. We are here today for a Status Conference in the case against Mr. Vojislav Seselj, and I would like to have the appearances. Prosecution first.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Good afternoon, Your Honour. For the Prosecution, Mr. Daniel Saxon and myself, Hildegard Uertz-Retzlaff, and we are together with our case manager, Ana Katalinic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Uertz-Retzlaff. For the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: My name is David Hooper of the bar of England and Wales. I am lead counsel in the case per the order of the Chamber of the 21st of August, 2006, and following the assignation, nomination, rather, by the Registry of the 31st of August, 2006. I have sitting with me here, to my left, immediate left, Dr. Andreas O'Shea, also of the bar of England and Wales. And I am assisted as a legal assistant by Lea Kulinowski, who sits toward the back of the court. I also take the opportunity to mention, he doesn't need to be formally introduced, Mr. Tjarda Van der Spoel, counsel assigned as stand-by counsel and whose status will be known to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the status of Mr. Van der Spoel being acting counsel for a period of 30 days, since the assignment of you, Mr. Hooper. By acting counsel, that means that he can act as counsel when you are not assigned yet. He of course would have to do it alone. But now he, I do see that he is involved in the appeal against the decision of this Chamber to --

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: Yes. His position as stand-by counsel ceased with my nomination and appointment. But the Registry have preserved his position in respect of the appeal which has now been -- the appeal that's been made against the order of this court of course to assign counsel, to assign effectively me in this case, that is presently subject to appeal. The appeal has been of course lodged and responded to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Hooper. I have a couple of matters on the agenda. The parties have informally informed about a few matters they would like to raise, and I, intend to give an opportunity to Mr. Seselj at the end of this hearing to address any health matters he might want to raise with me. The first issue I would like to --

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: Mr. President, just one moment. Sorry to interrupt you. My understanding is, at present, that Mr. Seselj would not have received the agenda in a language that he understands. And in those circumstances, as what I'm saying is being translated, I wonder whether it would be helpful if I just very quickly ran through the items of the agenda.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know exactly -- yes, the agenda which I have in front of me might not be exactly the same as yours, because I have some additional remarks which I would not expect you -- What is on the agenda is to revisit disclosure, to pay attention to trial-related matters, that we pay attention to 92 bis and adjudicated facts, that we pay attention to protective measures, that we pay attention to e-court and hard copies of exhibits, the accused's health and conditions of detention, and any other business raised by any of the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I would first like to turn to disclosure issues.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Orie, this man with a bird's nest on his head has been falsely introduced by you as my counsel. He will never be my Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, if you want to address me, or later on the Trial Chamber you can do so through counsel. If you don't wish to do that, you will not be able to address this Chamber apart from when I specifically allow you to address me as the Judge at this moment, as I indicated at the beginning of -- Mr. Seselj --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, Mr. Orie, I will not be taking part in this theatrical production. I'm not interested in your theatrical production. You have denied me my right to defend myself and you want me to serve here as an extra. I will not be an extra in the courtroom. You can conduct the trial without me, because you are an illegal tribunal anyway. You are acting in contravention of all human rights. You brought actors here to act as my Defence counsel. They are not my Defence counsel. They are your spies, and their task is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, it seems that you do not want to adhere to the decision this Chamber has taken. If you choose not to be present, that's at least what I hear, then you will not be able to follow this proceedings. You will not be able to consult with Mr. Hooper, whether there would be anything that should be raised on your behalf. Therefore, I suggest to you that it would be preferable that you stay, but if you don't want to do that, I'm not going to force you to stay in this courtroom, if you consider your presence of no value whatsoever, and the same will be true at later stages of the Tribunal -- later stages of the proceedings. So therefore, if you say, as you expressed earlier, that you don't want to serve here as an extra and if you feel you are here as an extra, you are not for me. You are the accused in this case. And I would very much like to hear, in accordance with the decision the Trial Chamber has taken, through counsel, whatever you would like to bring to the attention of me or, later, of this Chamber. But finally, the choice is yours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Hooper will never be able to do anything on my behalf, not a single step in the trial. Today, Mr. Orie, I submitted a request to the relevant judicial body. In accordance with it, you are duty-bound to immediately stay these proceedings until the request on your dismissal from the case is ruled upon. This morning I submitted that motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If this would have been a matter you would like to raise, you should have done it through Mr. Hooper. I am not, at this moment, expecting any further comments from you. If there is anything you think should be brought to my attention, you can do it through Mr. Hooper, but I understand that's not what you wish to do. I do not allow you to do it yourself, apart from the matter I mentioned earlier. And if --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm leaving the courtroom right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, I will not allow you to interrupt me all the times. If you decide that you wish to leave the courtroom, then I will instruct security to escort you out of the courtroom, and we will continue with this Status Conference --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Orie, be so kind and issue an order to have me escorted out of the courtroom, because I have nothing further to say to you. Hooper has no right to speak on my behalf.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: I am not getting translated, and that's because I'm unfamiliar with the channel system here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no, no, I can tell you why it is, because I pushed the priority button when I have not allowed Mr. Seselj to speak. What he says comes not through the microphone and will not be translated. That is because I did not allow Mr. Seselj to speak or to interrupt me, and if there is anything that should be put on the record which he wanted to say he should do it through you. I take it that the -- I have a priority button which excludes all microphones in this courtroom, apart from mine, and the interpreters are dependent on the microphones.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: Thank you. I am in fact getting a transcription in English, so I'm not unaware of what's being said. I make that plain. But I just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: I wondered what was being said, and I was also -- wondered what had happened to the Serbian translation, but now I know. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. So it has been translated despite me pushing the priority button. As a matter of fact, yes, I heard the translation as well. So I should have been aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Orie, will you be so kind and order the guards to escort me out of the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, Mr. Seselj. At this moment I am doing something else. Mr. Seselj, I will give you an opportunity which you might not wish to use, to consult with Mr. Hooper to inform him about what you said before about why we would have to stop these proceedings. If you don't take that opportunity, you may express your wish to leave the courtroom, then I will instruct security to escort you to the --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will never speak to Hooper, never in my life, or with any other spy of yours, whose goal it is to deny me my right to my defence. And therefore I am asking you to instruct the guards to escort me out of the courtroom, so that we avoid any excesses here, Mr. Orie. I am a very calm and balanced person, and I don't like any excessive behaviour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I interpret your request for me to instruct the guards to escort you out of the courtroom as an expression of your wish not to remain in this courtroom at this moment. So therefore, security, please --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Until you restore my right to defend myself, I will not be participating.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we will continue with this Status Conference, Mr. Seselj preferring not to be present and not accepting the decision of the Trial Chamber that he would be represented by counsel at and is at this moment not allowed, apart from the limits set by the Trial Chamber, to represent himself. Then we move on to disclosure. Let's go through it. The supporting material has been disclosed. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It has been disclosed. Mr. Hooper, usually disclosure is finished once it has been disclosed, but I would like to know whether you have received the supporting material, whether it's available to you. That's the supporting material on the Rule 66(A)(i).

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: Yes. So far as I know, and we've been very much assisted by Mr. Van der Spoel, all material that's been served on the Defence is now in my possession.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: Including the supporting material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I move on to a specific request. I do understand, Mr. Hooper, that you would very much like to have disclosed to you any statements given in domestic courts, earlier or statements that might be used that might be relevant for this case. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is the practice of the Prosecution to disclose such statements as part of the Prosecution's obligations under Rule 66(A)(ii). So we have been disclosing such statements where we have them in our possession and we will continue to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So what you are actually saying, what the Defence is asking for is already among the material disclosed?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Hooper, does that answer your request?

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: Yes, it does. And certainly if that intent is fulfilled, we'll be entirely satisfied. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If there were any -- I can imagine that it will take you some time to find your way through all the materials. If the Prosecution could assist Mr. Hooper and identify where to find the statements given in actual court proceedings, it would be highly appreciated. I take it anyhow that there will be some can contact between Prosecution and Defence in order to assist Mr. Hooper in getting acquainted with the case, as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution and Mr. Hooper and Mr. O'Shea have already met at least twice, so we are endeavouring to assist as much as we can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then next, Rule 68 material. That is then, to the extent disclosed, is available to you. At least that's what I understand from your earlier answer, Mr. Hooper. Then the next issue is the disclosure of material related to witnesses for whom an application for delayed disclosure is pending. And I do understand that the Prosecution wants to address me on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, very briefly. The Prosecution would like to reply to several points made by assigned Defence counsel recently in his response to the Prosecution's seventh and eighth motions for protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: With respect to paragraphs 2 through 6 of the assigned counsel's response, where assigned counsel argues that the Defence should receive the same information as the Trial Chamber with respect to information related to witnesses whom are the subject of pending motions for protective measures. As you know, the Statute, articles 20 and 22, obliges this Tribunal to be concerned, in addition to the fair trial rights of the accused, but also the interests and rights of victims and witnesses, particularly their safety and security. The Prosecution believes that to oblige the Prosecution to provide sensitive witness information to the Defence in the context of a motion for protective measures submitted before the start of a trial effectively would have absurd results because it would undermine our statutory obligations. Granting protective measures to Prosecution witnesses, including delayed disclosure does not disadvantage the Defence, so long as the Defence has sufficient time to prepare for -- to prepare to test the evidence given by Prosecution witnesses. Prosecution is not trying to obstruct the Defence's right to prepare for trial, nor is it trying to undermine the principle of equality of arms, but the Prosecution feels very strongly that it must, while protecting the accused's right to a fair trial, it must also fulfil its statutory obligation to protect the safety and security of victim witnesses. Paragraph 9 of the Defence response, there is an argument regarding the delicate balance that is necessary between the rights of the accused and the interests of the victim and witnesses and the need to create this balance by having proper regard to the particular circumstances of this proceeding. We agree with that comment, and we say that in the particular circumstances of this proceeding then delayed disclosure is perfectly appropriate. We are dealing here with an accused who has publicly declared his intention to destroy this Tribunal, who has constantly flouted and flaunted the Rules of this Tribunal, and who has already publicly harassed and intimidated Prosecution witnesses. So in this particular case, Your Honour, the Prosecution believes that the balance should be struck cautiously vis-a-vis exposing witnesses to risk. Paragraphs 11 to 12 the Defence response, the assigned counsel refers to a so-called common practice regarding the disclosure of witness statements and the identity of sensitive witnesses to the Defence and says that that common practice is that such statements should be disclosed 30 days prior to the commencement of trial. A party's burden when making an application for protective measures is laid out in the Brdjanin and Talic decisions from Judge Hunt from July of 2000, which was followed by the Milosevic Trial Chamber in February of 2002, and it says that the Prosecution must demonstrate that exceptional circumstances exist in order for delayed disclosure to be granted. In this case, given the particular circumstances, we feel we have met that burden. Regarding the so-called common practice of disclosure 30 days prior to the commencement of trial, there is an equal practice, whether it may be called common or not, Your Honour, at least in certain cases, with respect to certain sensitive witnesses of allowing disclosure of the witness's identity and their unredacted statements during the trial 30 days prior to testimony or even shorter. And I would refer the Chamber and the Defence, for example, to the testimony of Witness C-047 in the Milosevic case for whom disclosure was permitted ten days prior to the witness's testimony. That's a decision dated 13th of March, 2003. And also the decision of the so-called Vukovar 3 Trial Chamber regarding Witness P-024, where the disclosure was permitted 30 days prior to the witness's testimony. So if there may be a common practice of 30 days prior to the commencement of trial, equally, Your Honour, there is certainly a practice with respect to particular witnesses in particular cases of shortening that time-period to take into account the particular protection needs of the witnesses. That's all I have to say on this, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hooper, would you like to respond immediately? Or would you like to take more time and to respond in writing? The issue being 30 days of course. We're close to 30 days from the start of the trial already, so there would not be, it would not make much sense to make, to start arguing about whether it should be on the 20th of September or the 25th of September instead of the 1st of October. But the Prosecution takes the view that 30 days prior to testimony would be the practice to be followed here, although I didn't hear that it is common practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We agree that it's perhaps getting a fine distinction, subject of course to the trial date, which is a matter which I think may be raised at a later --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I can stop you. In order to leave no puzzle for you, the Chamber has in mind to schedule the start of the trial at the very beginning of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: Very well. In which case the response that we've already made to the Prosecution's seventh and eighth protective measures motion remains relevant, and the points there, I hope, unfairly made. And they're made of course in the context of this particular assignment and this particular short pre-trial period and with the demands on what is presently still a small Defence team, in respect of preparation in order to meet the Chamber's expectations for starting in early November. Mr. Saxon, I noticed, may, may perhaps have misunderstood to some extent the thrust of our request, for the reasons for the stringent measures that the Prosecution were invoking, and the reason for that is that there's, as we understand it, in those requests by the Prosecution a general statement that they're needed. But the reasons for such stringent measures are not in fact given. And it's our submission that the reasons could be given to the extent that they satisfy our enquiry, permitting us, in fact, to also assess and respond, and also for the Chamber, in fact, to assess and respond. But particularly us, put us in the picture, to the extent of justifying those stringent measures requested so that -- and to do that without, we think, defeating the object of the exercise, which is of course to protect witnesses. So we feel that the Prosecution can provide the reasons, without, as it were, removing the protection of the witness by revealing too much information. It is a question of how much they reveal. I think the only other matter we raised in that motion was, if there are redacted statements, can we have them? And I understand that certainly in respect of some of them the Prosecution argument is, well, if they're effectively redacted, there will be very little to read or nothing to read. But we would like that reviewed. And if it is possible, in the alternative, to application for immediate service of unredacted statements, that we have redacted statements. I don't add any more to the issue of common practice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, two clear questions. The one is, could you be a bit more specific on your reasons. That's one. And the second is, even if there is little to read, why not give then that at least to read to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, it would be, quite frankly, to provide the reasons for which each of our proposed witnesses require protective measures effectively would require the Prosecution to release its information explaining who each witness is and what their position is. So we don't see any difference, quite frankly, unless we were -- unless we were to provide some very generic reason such as, you know, the witness has exceptional security concerns, which obviously would not be terribly helpful to the Defence. With regard to the second question. The Prosecution submits that with respect to its so-called insider witnesses, for whom, whom are the subject of the majority of these protective measures, redactions would be, quite frankly, pointless and useless and a waste of time, because virtually the entire statement -- statements would have to be blacked out, and the result would be the Defence would have little or nothing to read. And that would not be useful for the Defence, nor would it be a useful use of the Prosecution's time and resources. There may be, Your Honour, one or two so-called crime-based witnesses for whom protective measures have been sought, for which some more reasons could be given without identifying the witness, for which, perhaps, a redacted statement could be provided. But the Prosecution will have to review that very carefully. But this would only apply to a very limited number of witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You say sometimes -- you couldn't say more than that the witness has security concerns. But sometimes witnesses have received threats by telephone or sometimes a witness is warned by others that someone is going after him. I mean, that of course would all fall within the scope of security concerns, but would be more specific. Is that -- Mr. Hooper, do I understand you well?

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You would like to have this kind of information, whether you say it's exclusively his position or it is supported by threats made already, or that's, to give even in abstract terms as much as possible to make it -- make you better able to assess the -- whether or not you would be inclined to respect the reasons or not to respect them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. It might be the simple position of someone being a member of an organisation whose position would immediately lead to identification. So the context of the statement, for example. But then there is other matters, such as you've raised, Mr. President, that add extra bite and assist us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Saxon, would you be willing -- there were several issues where you said you couldn't go any further than security concerns. Of course the Chamber will look at whether there would be a possibility to say more, and you're not only invited but urged to review that possibility in every respect on the seventh and the eighth motion, so that both the Defence is assisted in taking its position in respect of the motions, and also for the Chamber to see how serious you have been in accommodating the Defence in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. In order to do that, we will have to review the information that is contained in the ex parte submissions that were attached to these motions for protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And we will endeavour to do that as soon as practical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I expect you to do that within five working days from now on. Would that be possible?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Could you make it ten, Your Honour? We want to do this as carefully as we can because of the interests that are at stake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand that you want to be very cautious in this respect. At the same time, time is limited also for the Defence. I mean, the Chamber has to prepare a decision. Once you've given this additional information, the Defence should be in a position to further respond on that information and we are coming closer and closer to the beginning of November. So five days. If you would not be able to do it within five days, you can show good cause why you were not. So five working days from now on to review the reasons on the basis of which you asked for protective measures and to disclose whatever could possibly be disclosed to the Defence. Then I am going back to the agenda. By the way, Mr. Hooper, any need to further say anything about this? Or shall we just wait and see?

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: No. No. Thank you. I thank the Prosecution too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I will move on to the trial-related matters. The start of the case is envisaged for early November 2006. And the Pre-Trial Conference to be held in due course before the commencement of trial. And usually, Mr. Hooper, sometimes in this Tribunal it was even on the same day or the day before or two days before. That's the -- perhaps the same day is not a good idea. Perhaps one or two days prior to the start of the trial would be the best idea. Yes? Yes. Of course there is one issue. We do not have yet the Appeals Chamber's decision on the appeal that is lodged against the decision of this Chamber to assign counsel. We all hope, and to be quite honest I do expect, that the Appeals Chamber will give its decision before the scheduled start of the trial. Of course the Appeals Chamber certainly will be aware of the urgency involved. The next trial issue, Madam Uertz-Retzlaff is the request of the Chamber, I should say the invitation of the Chamber to reduce the scope of the indictment. The Chamber has received your response, in which you say: We cannot follow your invitation, but if you -- I think you said request us to do it, we will then come up with a new submission. Of course, under the Rules, we could even direct you to that. But the Chamber would very much appreciate having read your response, that you give it an effort to file within one week from now on what you would have filed if the Chamber would have required you to make such a new submission.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, let me -- please allow me to make two points.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: First of all, as you have seen from our submission that the primary argument of the Prosecution is that this indictment is already streamlined --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: -- according to the needs of an expeditious trial, and that the estimate of the Prosecution case is actually six months.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I come to that in more detail soon, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And for an accused of this level of leadership and responsibility, that is indeed a very expeditious trial. And therefore, actually, as we have already indicated in paragraph 10 of our submission, we would urge the Trial Chamber not to require the reduction of the scope of the indictment at this point in time, but rather address this issue after the first six or two months that we are in trial, so that we can see whether our expectations are met.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: My second point is the following. The accused is not just a member of a JCE that acts in always the same way in huge number of municipalities. The situation in each of the named municipalities that we have addressed in the indictment is quite specific as to the goals of the accused and the other JCE members and the means employed. It is not an indictment charging the very same criminal conduct in a huge amount of municipalities. And it is also not a case of a remote perpetrator far away from any of these crime bases, such as, for instance, Slobodan Milosevic. Instead, we have an accused who physically commits or instigates some of the crimes charged. One can definitely not drop a crime base in which the accused himself appears to be the physical perpetrator or the direct instigator of the crimes, that is at least the position of the Prosecution. And then the question is: Which one of the other few municipalities to drop and still have the ability to present the scope and conduct of the criminality of this accused? The Prosecution, therefore, rather did not like to drop a municipality, or incidence, because it would cut into the core of the -- of this case against the accused. In paragraph 29 of our submission, we have indicated our willingness to drop counts, meaning alternative charges; for instance, as an example, the Counts 2 and 3 and -- or the Counts 6 and 7. But of course we do not know whether the Trial Chamber would actually find that sufficient. And what we want to make clear is that we are not making a proposal to drop or reduce parts from our indictment voluntarily. We would, of course, do it if the Trial Chamber direct us to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: So if you direct us to do so, we can indeed prepare a proposal for these reductions, and -- but I would request to get a time-frame until one week from now, that's the 21st of September, because if we have to drop substantial, if we are forced to do so, if we have to cut into the substance of the case, we have to carefully really consider that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Uertz-Retzlaff, isn't it true that if the Chamber invites you to cut the case to two-thirds, it would always have an impact on your ability to present the scope and the conduct of the criminality of this accused, as you said. I mean, isn't that inherent to our invitation? You say, well, if we would have to do that, we would not -- we could not present the full scope of his behaviour and conduct. It very much now seems to become a question of, if we cut it down further it would not present the scope of the responsibility or the conduct or of the criminality, whatever you call it, but isn't it true that is always a matter of more or less?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, you are correct. But I think in this particular case, it's quite different from other leadership cases that have already been heard here in this Tribunal, because we have heard leadership cases where, let's say, the -- always the same conduct in, let's say, up to 20, 30 municipalities was actually the Prosecution case and evidence was heard about. But here, when you look at the nine municipalities, you will find charged different conduct. For instance, let me just take the municipality of Brcko. For instance, in relation to the municipality of Brcko, we did not charge the murders and the ethnic cleansing practices applied per se. We only picked one particular camp because we want to show the, in particular, forced labour aspects of this case and the sexual assaults of this case. Or for instance in relation to Bjeljina. You will also find that the focus of the charges in relation to Bjeljina is basically forced labour, sexual assaults and the like, and it is not that we charged for each and every indictment the full scale of the ethnic cleansing means that were applied. That's what I mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: So if we, for instance, cut certain municipalities, we will lose whole chapters of criminal conduct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, just to -- you said in Brcko we did not charge everything, we charged forced labour and sexual assaults. I think you said for Bjeljina we did the same. Of course the question would then be, if you would do that for Brcko, would it -- would the case be totally different if we would not do it anymore for Bjeljina? I mean, to what extent is more of the same behaviour ...

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have -- we have actually listed, in our submissions, the municipalities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I see that here.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. And you will find there is a difference, always a difference in conduct and, in particular, also a difference in associates of the accused appearing on the scene and committing the crimes. For Bjeljina, for instance, we have Vojvoda Mirko Blagojevic responsible for the crimes. And here in Bjeljina, we have a municipality where, in addition to the abuse of civilians in detention facilities, we have the deliberate destruction of separate sites which is the focus for the Bjeljina municipality which you would not find in Brcko and you would not find in other municipalities that we have charged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I do understand that it's not all the same, Madam Uertz-Retzlaff. But the issue is whether -- not whether what you would like to keep is exactly the same, but sometimes it might be slightly different, perhaps with other persons. But nevertheless what -- I mean, you have done the same exercise. You could perhaps have taken other municipalities as well and other participants in the joint criminal enterprise as well. So you cut that down. What makes you believe that it would be these I think nine municipalities and we could not do with seven, and that it's essential that we include an issue where Mr. Blagojevic was involved in the joint criminal enterprise? Of course we have read your response, but I am not convinced yet. But I am not the only Judge in this Chamber. We are the three of us.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, Your Honours, we actually embarked with our submission to show to the Trial Chamber, to demonstrate that each of these municipalities are unique and it's not a repetition of crimes being committed in the area, and that's why we felt we can't really drop any of those. We wouldn't know which one, because all of them are of great importance for this case. But as I said, if you direct us to do that, we will of course do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Uertz-Retzlaff, you would follow such directive. Mr. Hooper, is there anything you would like to add on this subject?

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: Essentially, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hooper. I would be interested, however, Madam Uertz-Retzlaff, because the Chamber will have to give a decision, to perhaps hear a bit more about your 100 court days expectation expressed in your response. You said: "We could present our case in six months approximately, 100 court days." Would that include cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We have actually based this calculation -- and I have done it a couple of times --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: -- according to how the witness list developed, we have calculated the six months on the basis of a five days week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Four hours taking of evidence each day. That's the basis. And we have actually included the time for cross-examination in it. And when you look at the witness list that we have provided, the figures given there are actually including the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We will, as I've said last time, is that we, of course, want to present the Prosecution case, the evidence in-chief mostly in writing, even related to the acts and conduct of the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And for that you may have seen already our first 89(F) motion, a series of these motions will follow, and it will be -- we have explained what we intend to do in that very first motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, how did you calculate the time for cross-examination if you call a witness under Rule 89(F), and what was your starting point on 92 bis witnesses? I mean, how did you calculate that? Because I see now that you say we more and more want to present our evidence under Rule 89(F), which means only a few questions and mainly the statement. That certainly reduces considerably the time taken by examination-in-chief. But what's, then, the key for calculating how much time would be needed for cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, we had actually looked at all the specific witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And have looked at each of them and made a calculation, and for the insiders, when 89(F) is allowed, we would actually take them only one to two hours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: -- in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: -- and the rest, when you for instance look at our witness list, you find for one witness, 17 for instance, eight hours, that would mean two hours examination-in-chief, six hours in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: So the majority of the time given is actually for cross-examination. And that same applies for the 92 bis witnesses, where we actually would just take ten minutes in-chief and have the rest in cross-examination time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take it, Mr. Hooper, that you had no opportunity yet to assess the -- how realistic the time assessed for cross-examination would be?

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: No, not at all. And with the particular feature of the case that was perhaps demonstrated today, that's another added unknown of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: So I am afraid we can't assist. We're not in a position to assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would you be in a position to, perhaps at random, to look at the witness list, pick out a few, and check perhaps on the basis of what of these examples, on whether you consider it realistic, the time. I mean, for example, I'm not saying that this is the case, but for example if you would have 400 pages of 92 bis (D) material, that's transcript from other cases, that if four hours were assessed for cross-examination, you would say no, I would need at least double. I'm trying to find out how realistic the time estimate is, because the Chamber, Madam Uertz-Retzlaff, is very much hesitant to proceed and then find out, which often happens, at a later stage, that the expectations are not met. Not to say that you could foresee that already, but we would rather be more certain on from the beginning that we'll meet the expectations, rather than to give it a try and then perhaps have to face a disappointment.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, we had a little bit of, at least in relation to the examination-in-chief, we have of course the example in the Milosevic case that I am familiar with where the examination-in-chief was often very, very short, because of 89(F) or 92 bis. The time taken for cross-examination was, in contrast to that, very extensive, but this depended on the accused, who defended himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And didn't focus. So I would expect that the Defence will focus on the issues that really matters and not on political points.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You say they might even take more time?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No. I think they will take less, much less. Because the Defence will know, a proper Defence will know what to focus on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm just saying that if you have a different focus, that doesn't automatically mean that it takes less time. That's --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I was comparing it only to the case, to the Milosevic case where the focus of the accused was quite a different one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Mr. Hooper, my request to you was whether you would, at random, try to take a sample and to see whether there is any realism in the approach taken by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: I couldn't do that today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no, no, I'm not asking you to do it today.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: But I will certainly try and assist the Chamber to get as accurate and objective a viewpoint of trial time and witness time by the end of this month, if possible. But it's difficult --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: Because we're not let into the case at all at the moment and we're not assisted at the moment, and we might never be, by the accused. So all I can say is that we will just need time. I'm sorry, I can't say more than that at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand. At the same time, this does not -- I mean, these are two, two exercises first, the reduction of the indictment, and a realistic assessment of the time needed for case presentation. So I would -- if you would commit yourself to at least look at a sample by the end of this month, then, Madam Uertz-Retzlaff, we might continue with the other exercise at the same time. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because whether or not reduced, it would have the same -- well, I wouldn't say problem. We would have the same issue of carefully assessing how much time we would need for case presentation. Then I would like to --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, before you move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I actually had a matter related to the commencement of trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: That I actually wanted to raise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Because it came up in the discussions that we had with Defence counsel and his team. The Prosecution has, in fact, already a list of the witness order in which it wants to call its witnesses, and we have already shared this list with the Victims and Witness Unit because a lot of protective measures needs and practical things have to be made. The 11 first witnesses are all insider witnesses, and most of them are called as so-called viva voce witnesses, but we will bring for all of them an 89(F) submission in the form that you have one already. And the question is whether the Defence, and they have addressed it with us, is able to actually deal with such an intense start of the trial, and Mr. Hooper had raised some concerns, and probably it's better to discuss it now because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, as a matter of fact, the next item on my agenda was whether we would have five days a week hearing programme, or whether it would be, as I do understand, less. I also understood that the Defence would request a four-day week to manage the material. I don't know whether, on the basis of your discussions with Madam Uertz-Retzlaff, Mr. Hooper, whether it is still the same?

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, we might even go for less. But realistically our application is that we sit for four days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber has been informed about this request. It has not decided upon it yet, but has considered it, and is wondering whether, if that would be the schedule, well, let's say, for until after the Christmas recess, whether that would already help you out at a level acceptable?

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: Yes. It would. And it could be subject to review.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, you will understand, Mr. Hooper, that the Chambers are seeking to use our facilities as efficiently as possible. Of course, never at the expense of the fairness of the trial, but nevertheless we are trying to accommodate the parties to the extent possible, and at the same time, we urge the parties, and ourselves, to do whatever we can to not have these courtrooms empty and not leave time unused which is available to us. From the mere fact that I say would that help you out, you could understand that we have understanding for the problems you are facing in the present situation. You said, of course, subject to review. Of course. And nothing is ever for certain, but we will then further consider that, that at least such a limited period of time in which we would be sitting not the full five days a week, would accommodate you at a level which would make it workable, if to say. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I please continue --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: -- with one point that I would like to make?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It relates also actually to the protective measures as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We have -- we want to take the insiders first because, first of all, it's logical as we think. But secondly, this order is needed under the -- this order is needed under witness protection aspects, and I would like to go into private session briefly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We will turn into private session, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in private session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, the (redacted) witnesses are most vulnerable as we think for intimidation in the time-period between disclosure of the identity to the Defence and the actual testimony. And I am not suggesting here that the Defence would disclose information. I am not suggesting that at all, and I do not expect that at all. The Defence, however, has to disclose the names of these particular witnesses to its investigative staff, and they, in turn, will have to start to ask questions about these people in the region, and that's how we fear their identity will get at least known to certain people, including the police, and that means, from then on, the witnesses would be in a risk, in a risk situation. The Prosecution, therefore, has scheduled the (redacted), the most vulnerable (redacted) for the first period of time in this trial, so that this particular sensitive time-period is as short as possible. In addition, certain temporary protective measures that I am not able to address right here now in the presence of the Defence cannot be kept in place for months and months and months. It can only be kept in place for a very limited time-period. Therefore, we would like to stick to this witness order that we have in mind, and if the Defence could not meet that, we should know that now, in advance. And it is definitely something that is of importance. And if the Trial Chamber and the Defence would agree to have that 30 days before testimony models of delayed disclosure, that would definitely be helpful and we would be then much more flexible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now we are talking about four days a week sitting. So starting at, I wouldn't say a slow pace but at least a slower pace than usual, would that seriously interfere with what you had in mind, as far as the (redacted) witnesses are concerned?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: If we could still start with them? Of course there is a delay, then, certainly. But I think it wouldn't be such a problem, if they -- but if the Defence, of course, would, for instance, after the first (redacted) stand up and say now we need a month to prepare this and the cross-examination can only take place later on, then we really would have a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand that. How many days are scheduled for these (redacted) witness, the first, what did you say, 11, I think, including cross?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would now actually have to count. The first 11, about 22 days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 22 days. So that should be easily be finished before the Christmas recess?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If we start early November, even if at a pace of four days a week, you say 22 days. That would be November -- well, let's say, apart from opening statements, another three and a half weeks, which would be 14 days and then the -- yes. 14 days and another 8 days that would bring us into the first two weeks of December. It would just fit, because I think the Christmas recess starts at mid-December, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour think it is the 18th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So four days a week. And then of course it might be very important for you, Mr. Hooper to know as early as possible who these witnesses would be so that you are able to start preparing for them immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: Yes, that is our concern, about the request for the order. And we have made our responses in respect to the seventh and eighth seeking of protective measures, our responses to that. And I don't add anything more to that, to that today. But in the context of the ordering of witnesses in the trial, we have, as you know, or may know, asked the Prosecution not to call (redacted) witnesses straight off, because it would put a considerable strain on our resources and our abilities to effect a fair trial, in our view, and that there are alternative witnesses that could be called, crime base witnesses for example that would, in fact, involve less of a potential of damage to fair trial if called at the outset of the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's a different balance to strike.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I think, first of all, one of the things before we turn into open session again, Madam Uertz-Retzlaff, one of the issues would be that if we would not finish -- if we would start with the (redacted) witnesses, if we would not finish before the Christmas recess, there would be an extension of additional protective measures, which you did not want to elaborate upon, which I fully understand, for another three weeks anyhow. Yes, let's turn into open session again.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Madam Registrar. I would very much like to urge the parties to see whether they can reach an agreement on what type of witnesses to start with, and whether it should be a monolithic block of one type of witnesses or a monolithic block of another type of witnesses, or whether it could be a couple of crime base witnesses first, and then the whole block of another type of witnesses. Because of course we could decide the matter, since even the order is -- order of presenting evidence is under the supervision of the Chamber. But if the parties could come to an agreement on this matter, I think that would be, by far, preferable from the Chamber imposing an order on this matter, not knowing exactly to what extent harm would be done to one interest or to another. So therefore the parties are urged to see whether any agreement could be reached on this matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any other matter in this respect?

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: Yes. One matter. The final witness list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Hooper has the final witness list. The only -- it's the final witness list that we filed with the Court. And of course we can never exclude that suddenly a witness shows up we don't know about yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And that is, of course, something that will always happen in each trial if something comes up. It will happen to us. It may happen to the Defence. So that cannot be excluded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But, indeed, you have the witness list. What always -- also happens, and I have that experience, that a witness dies, a witness that -- or a witness gets sick and needs to be replaced. That can never be excluded from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no, of course, that goes without saying, Madam Uertz-Retzlaff. I do understand the list is as final as possible under the circumstances. I stress that if you say so, Madam Uertz-Retzlaff, that the Chamber relies upon this information, because I have experienced situations where the final witness list was updated almost on a weekly basis, of course I'm exaggerating, but for both parties I would say make these lists such that we can work with them and not just them being a mere guess or speculation. But I trust that you have given sufficient attention to that. Mr. Hooper, so you have the list? Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: Yes. We have the list. I think the point, and it's well made by Mr. O'Shea in my ear there, is that if it is endorsed, as it were, by the Chamber as the final witness list, then it means that the Prosecution can only move a further witness through a motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: And that's our understanding of the position. I'm grateful to my friend on the other side for nodding so that we know where we are at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At the same time you will understand that our ongoing, I wouldn't say dispute but our ongoing conversation with the Prosecution on the reduction of the -- might influence the finality of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: Indeed. We're encouraged smaller rather than larger in any event, and we understand that, yes. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the next issue I have on my agenda. I think it can be very brief on that. I don't know how important or relevant it still is, but I think the Defence has asked for further interpretation of the Chamber's order that the accused is not allowed to represent himself and the Defence request whether it is able to defer a trial to the accused, let's assume that he once appears. To defer a trial, the Chamber has, I think, clearly indicated in its order that Mr. Seselj's participation in the proceedings will be through counsel unless, having heard from counsel, the Chamber determines otherwise. So we would need to hear from you why it is necessary for the accused to take the floor in a specific situation before we will consider that. Mr. Hooper, that's slightly different from how you seem to have understood our order.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: I do see the order certainly in that way, because it's expressed in that way, that Mr. Seselj will, in fact, participate in this trial through counsel. The real position is, it certainly will assist us if in addressing the interface or modalities, as it were, of Mr. Seselj's participation in the case, if I may express, as I have in fact already, or I can express now, a possible way in which this might develop. Now, first of all, I acknowledge as assigned counsel that this question of deferring to an accused or to this accused will be done only, of course, through the Chamber and with the permission of the Chamber. But it may be possible for all of that for me to be able to say, well, we're in this position. Let's imagine that the first witness has been called and given his or her evidence in-chief. And the moment comes now for the Defence to cross-examine that witness. Now, with either particular leave in respect of that witness, or perhaps even as a general principle, subject to one other matter I will come to in a moment, it would be commensurate with my function for me, in fact, to get to my feet, but before I questioned that witness to defer to the accused in order -- with the leave of the Court to give him the opportunity of putting those matters that he wishes to to the witness. Now, I do that in circumstances where it may be that Mr. Seselj will not want to provide me with instructions, so that's the basis of that. Now, what would happen then? Well, Mr. Seselj would have his opportunity to put those questions, if he doesn't want to instruct me, at least to be able to put those important matters to the witness that he feels needs to be put. Of course, this is all conditional on the view that the Chamber takes of his behaviour. As assigned counsel, I come into the case knowing that the Chamber has taken a particular view that's led to an assignment of counsel in this case. And I recognise that. That when it comes to trial, if the accused is given that opportunity, it may satisfy certain, certain matters that otherwise will be a difficulty, a lack of instructions perhaps for example, in my case. As I see that order, this is not an order that should be interpreted as shutting out Mr. Seselj from the trial. Not at all. And this would be perhaps a way forward. But it would be very much conditional on him participating, if such deferment is allowed, within normal expectations of behaviour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Hooper, the Chamber has considered this matter and would not allow. If Mr. Seselj refuses to give you instructions, and if you do not receive relevant information which would allow you to cross-examine the first witness, then the Chamber will not, for these reasons, allow Mr. Seselj to conduct the cross-examination. It is on the basis of the behaviour of Mr. Seselj until now in these proceedings and on the basis of the other reasons given in the decision of this Chamber, that the Chamber does not wish Mr. Seselj to continue to represent himself. And allowing him, as the first one, to cross-examine a witness, disregarding what the Chamber imposed upon him, that is that he should conduct his Defence through counsel, is not acceptable to the Chamber. This is not to exclude, as I said, today I said to Mr. Seselj if there is any health issue he may address the Chamber directly. This is not to exclude not at a certain moment -- let me say the following without even suggesting that I'm deciding matters at this moment. In another case before the Tribunal, a Chamber which I presided over, allowed the accused to put questions, and the accused, who was represented, to put questions to a witness in addition to the cross-examination by counsel if, for any specific reason, the accused was better placed or would be in a better position to put a follow-up question because of his very specific knowledge. However, for the protection of the material, there is no rule which automatically continues its application in the next case. So what I would expect, as a matter of fact, is that if you do not need any further protective measures as far as the persons are concerned, that it's there, and that as far as protection of the material is concerned -- but you're talking about witnesses, but Article 70 has got nothing to do with witnesses has got mainly to do with material, and then of course has some consequences for witnesses called in relation to that material. For those witnesses, I would say the protective measures would still apply, but for the material you should make an application to make that material -- to make that material protected under Rule 70, because if a witness is protected, it could be a closed session, it could be anything. But the protection of a witness does not exclude to put certain questions to that witness. That's not part of the protective measures. However, it could be a consequence of the protection of material. And therefore if you would like to have this same effective protection both of the witness and of the material, you should apply for the protection of the material, whereas no application needs to be made for the person of the witness, unless you think that it is an incorrect statement of the law, of course, I would like -- this is not a decision. I just gave you my interpretation of Rules 70 and 75. If you would you disagree, please tell me.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I only wanted to raise that it is not a very complex motion. The two witnesses are not insider witnesses, and we would, actually, prefer to have a very early decision on that. We can use this 89(F) procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You include that, and Mr. Hooper, you are trying to seek an agreement with the Prosecution on that. If not, the request is there. You would like to have until the 14th of October and -- so if we don't hear from you, well, let's say, within -- until next week, Wednesday, we will give the decision whether you have until the 14th of October. If we hear prior to that from you, then --

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: All right thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- the Chamber will consider to adopt what you agreed upon. Anything else?

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: No other matters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I realise time is pressing. Very, very briefly. The Prosecution would simply encourage the Defence, as soon as possible, to arrange with the Registry to get an account on the electronic disclosure system, the EDS. We think that will facilitate both -- the work of both parties, both the Prosecution and the Defence, that if there are collections of material that can be made available they can access via the Internet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know if you know what it is Mr. Hooper, yes or no, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: I'm afraid I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You applied for an account to be -- to get that as soon as possible?

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: Do I need to do that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's what I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: Well, it's a Registry matter, and I think it's a question of being keyed into it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We have one minute to go, but it will be taken care of, that you will not be deprived from any electronic disclosure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there is nothing else, we will adjourn. I thank very much the interpreters and the technicians for their indulgence to stay for all of this time. One small advantage is that we don't have to resume. We adjourn sine die.
